The European Parliament has approved a new directive on payment services and electronic money services in the EU's internal market. The vote was 484 in favour, 8 against, with 118 abstentions. The directive would replace two earlier directives (2015/2366/EU and 2009/110/EC) and makes some changes to Directive 98/26/EC.

The rules cover who may offer payment and electronic money services in the EU and how those businesses are supervised. A company that wants to offer these services must get authorisation from the authorities in its home Member State. Its application has to include a plan of the services it intends to offer, proof that it holds the required starting capital, and a description of how it protects customers' money. It must also explain how it manages the business and controls its risks, how it handles security incidents and customer complaints, how it protects sensitive payment data, and how it would keep operating in an emergency. The company must also name its directors and major shareholders, show that they are suitable, and provide a plan for winding up the business if it fails. It must additionally describe its audit arrangements and how it protects users and keeps its services reliable.

Payment institutions must hold starting capital of at least EUR 25,000, EUR 50,000 or EUR 150,000, depending on the services they provide. Their own funds may not fall below that starting capital or the other required amount. Authorisation is granted if the applicant is a legal person established in a Member State and has the required capital. Authorities must tell applicants within two months of receiving an application whether it has been approved, and must give reasons if it is refused.

An authorisation is valid throughout the EU. The home authority can withdraw it only if the firm has not used it within twelve months of obtaining it, or has not provided any of the authorised services for more than six consecutive months. Member States must keep public registers of payment institutions, and the European Banking Authority (EBA) must run a central electronic register.

Firms that outsource operational tasks must tell their home authorities. They may not outsource important operational functions, including ICT systems, in a way that weakens their internal controls or prevents regulators from monitoring their compliance. Each Member State must name the authorities responsible for authorising and supervising payment institutions. These may be public authorities or bodies recognised by national law, including national central banks. The directive also sets out rules for firms that want to operate in other Member States, whether by setting up there or by providing services across borders, and includes transitional provisions.
